title: Youi names Australia’s riskiest driving hour
full_text:
Youi says 3pm is Australia’s most stressful and incident-prone driving hour, with 55% of drivers surveyed naming it the peak pressure point on the road and 24% reporting a road incident during the afternoon rush in the past year.
The insurer’s Project 3PM study surveyed 2,334 drivers in August, and its findings were first reported that month before being issued in September. Nearly half (48%) of respondents are on the road around 3pm on three or more weekdays a week, citing shopping (40%), appointments (29%), work travel (24%), the journey home (22%) and school pick-up (17%). Youi said its claims data showed more road incidents around 3pm than any other hour.
Youi’s description of the study says “incident” includes near misses, collisions and loss of vehicle control, so the 24% is not a count of crashes.
“The research shows 3pm isn’t just another busy traffic period. It’s the point in the day where work, family and household responsibilities all converge, creating a unique pressure point for drivers,” said Marni Jackson, Youi’s head of product for vehicle and lifestyle. “What’s particularly concerning is that respondents reporting higher levels of pressure were more likely to report risky driving behaviours behind the wheel. The reality is that 3pm isn’t simply a traffic problem. It’s a pressure problem.”
While 84% of respondents rate their own driving as safe during the 3pm rush, only 42% extend that confidence to other drivers. Respondents were more likely to blame another driver’s behaviour (44%) for an incident than rushing (26%), fatigue (22%) or mobile phone use (19%).
Forty-three per cent (43%) said they feel too fatigued or mentally drained to concentrate fully around 3pm. When running late, 62% admitted to risky driving behaviours: 28% become impatient with other drivers, 20% change lanes more often, 19% accelerate through amber lights and 18% exceed the speed limit. Gen Z drivers reported the highest incident rate at 42%, followed by Millennials at 30%, while parents of school-aged children reported higher fatigue and incident exposure.
About half of respondents said drivers play the most important role in improving road safety. A quarter chose better school pick-up zone management as the change most likely to reduce afternoon stress, followed by leaving earlier (23%), safer road and school-zone infrastructure (22%) and better route planning (18%).
Youi developed a 3PM Playbook with Road Sense Australia, whose chief executive Michael Fitzgibbins said recognising pressure before driving is one of the simplest safety steps. “Simple actions such as planning ahead, reducing distractions, putting your phone away and allowing extra travel time can make a meaningful difference,” he said. “The safest decision during the 3pm rush is often made before the engine even starts.”
Youi said the survey, run by Ideally on Aug. 4 and 5, has not been independently verified and may not be representative of the general population.
The study lands as road safety and pricing both face scrutiny. The Bureau of Infrastructure and Transport Research Economics recorded 1,326 road deaths in the 12 months to July 2026.
On pricing, coverage of ASIC’s disclosure findings shows car insurance premiums rose 8% in the 12 months to July 2025, against 3% for consumer prices, and that the regulator found insurers generally did not explain why premiums changed in quote and renewal documents. The publication reported that brokers who walk clients through the drivers, including repair costs, vehicle technology and natural disaster costs, supply what insurer notices often do not. The Insurance Council of Australia says repair bills make up roughly 60% of claim costs.
Youi’s data adds a behavioural angle to that conversation, giving brokers a concrete, time-specific risk to raise with clients who regularly drive the afternoon school and shopping run. Youi did not say whether the findings will influence its pricing or underwriting.
